prompt: Marina's analysis was correct and nothing was decided. What does the lesson blame?
hint: Look at what the slides asked the room to do.

choices.text: The data she joined
choices.why: The joins were checked and the numbers held; lesson 10 even tests the strongest objection.

choices.text: Too little time
choices.why: Eleven minutes is enough for one clear finding. Time was short for decoding, not for deciding.

choices.text: An audience that does not care about churn
choices.why: They cared enough to ask questions. They were never given a reason to act.

choices.text: Slides that left the analysis to the audience
choices.why: The tables were raw material: the room had to divide and compare, row by row, in eleven minutes.

prompt: Which title would have done the most work for the room?
hint: A title can be a label or a sentence.

choices.text: First-delivery analysis, H1 2025
choices.why: That names the topic. The reader still has to find the finding.

choices.text: Cancellations by cohort, region and first delivery
choices.why: A list of the table's columns, longer and no more useful.

choices.text: Late first deliveries more than double early cancellations
choices.why: It is the finding as a sentence: somebody who reads only the title has the point.

choices.text: Data quality notes
choices.why: Useful in an appendix; it says nothing about what was found.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson say a meeting is short of? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three things, and data is not one of them.

choices.text: Attention
choices.why: Six items in forty minutes; decoding loses.

choices.text: Meaning
choices.why: A number is not yet a reason to act.

choices.text: A request
choices.why: Without one, the room does the default: nothing.

choices.text: More data
choices.why: Marina brought thirty-eight slides of it.

prompt: Put the three questions in the order an analysis should answer them.
hint: From the fact to the action.

prompt: Match each sentence about Faro to the question it answers.
hint: Information, insight, decision.

pairs.left: 17.3% of new subscribers got their first box late
Run a pilot that fixes the first delivery in one region

prompt: Why do analysts stop at the first of the three questions, by the lesson?
hint: Think about risk, in public.

choices.text: Because the other two are the manager's job
choices.why: The lesson argues the opposite: a room left to supply them supplies them badly.

choices.text: It is the answer they are sure of
choices.why: The data says 17.3% and nobody argues. The other two are claims that might be wrong.

choices.text: Software reports stop there
choices.why: Software does stop there, but the lesson's reason is about the analyst.

choices.text: Because a recommendation would be biased by definition
choices.why: A recommendation is a claim to be tested, not a bias. Lesson 9 is about writing one.

prompt: Sandra heard "some first deliveries are late" and concluded it was noise. Which question did she answer for Marina?
hint: Marina left one of the three open.

choices.text: What?
choices.why: Marina had answered that one herself: 17.3% late.

choices.text: So what?
choices.why: Deciding that it does not matter is an answer to why it matters, supplied by the person with most reason to supply it.

choices.text: Now what?
choices.why: Nobody reached a decision; the room moved on.

choices.text: Who is responsible?
choices.why: Not one of the three, and not what she said.

prompt: A deck of thirty slides answers only What?. What does the lesson say to do with it?
hint: It may be a very good document.

choices.text: Send it as a report rather than presenting it
choices.why: A report is read at the reader's pace; a presentation needs So what? and an ending on Now what?.

choices.text: Delete half of the slides
choices.why: Fewer slides of the same kind are still a report.

choices.text: Present it faster
choices.why: Speed does not supply meaning or a request.

choices.text: Add an agenda slide at the start to guide the room through every table in order
choices.why: An agenda orders the tables; it does not say what they mean.

prompt: What did the 2007 study by Small, Loewenstein and Slovic find when statistics were added to one girl's story?
hint: It went the opposite way from what an analyst would hope.

choices.text: Donations fell compared with the story alone
choices.why: That is the finding. The lesson draws a narrower rule from it: a case gets attention an aggregate does not.

choices.text: Donations rose
choices.why: They fell compared with the story alone.

choices.text: Nothing changed
choices.why: There was a difference, and it went down.

choices.text: People trusted the charity more
choices.why: The study measured giving, not trust.

prompt: You have the 41.5% and want a case to make it real. Which case should you pick?
hint: The number chooses the case, not the other way round.

choices.text: The angriest complaint in the inbox this month, because anger is what a room remembers
choices.why: Vivid and untypical: it persuades the room of something the number does not say.

choices.text: No case at all, because a single customer is an anecdote and anecdotes are not evidence
choices.why: A case that the number describes is legitimate; it buys the attention the number needs.

choices.text: A customer whose first box was days late and who cancelled weeks later
choices.why: It is what the number describes, so the case illustrates the evidence instead of replacing it.

choices.text: Your own experience as a customer
choices.why: Nothing says you are typical, and it invites the room to answer with theirs.

prompt: "1,058 late first deliveries in six months." What does the lesson say the sentence lacks?
hint: Is that a lot?

choices.text: More precision than a count of whole deliveries
choices.why: It is precise to the unit.

choices.text: A source that a sceptic in the room could check
choices.why: The source matters, but it is not what this sentence lacks.

choices.text: Decimal places, so the rate can be read exactly
choices.why: More digits would make it harder, not easier.

choices.text: A scale the listener already holds
choices.why: "One new subscriber in six" gives the same fact a ruler.

prompt: Why did the finding have no natural owner in Marina's meeting?
hint: Whose number was the churn, and whose the delay?

choices.text: It crossed two departments, and the churn owner was absent
choices.why: Logistics owned the cause and marketing the effect; the room held only the side whose measure said all was well.

choices.text: Marina had not been in the company long
choices.why: That affects trust, a different problem in the same section.

choices.text: Nobody in the room had a budget for delivery or for marketing campaigns
choices.why: Paulo owns the delivery budget.

choices.text: Cancellations are a finance number, reported to the finance director every month
choices.why: In this story the cancellation rate was the marketing director's.

prompt: How many new subscribers joined Faro between January and June 2025?
hint: Add the subscribers column.

prompt: To one decimal place, what percentage of late-first-delivery customers cancelled within 90 days?
Sandra reports 94.5% of deliveries on time; Marina reports 17.3% of first deliveries late. Which is correct?
hint: They measure different deliveries.

choices.text: Sandra's, because it covers more deliveries
choices.why: Covering more deliveries makes it a different measure, not a truer one.

choices.text: Marina's, because it is more recent
choices.why: Both cover the same six months.

choices.text: Neither, until the two are reconciled
choices.why: There is nothing to reconcile; each is right about what it counts.

choices.text: Both
choices.why: One counts every delivery, the other only first ones. Lesson 2 builds the story on that apparent contradiction.

prompt: Who owns the budget for delivery at Faro?
hint: He chairs the meeting.

choices.text: Sandra, head of logistics
choices.why: She runs the team; the budget sits above her.

choices.text: Renata, finance
choices.why: She thinks in margin and payback; the delivery budget is Paulo's.

choices.text: Paulo, director of operations
choices.why: He chairs the meeting and owns the delivery budget.

choices.text: Ligeiro, the carrier that makes most of the deliveries
choices.why: An outside company with its own contract.

prompt: In the spreadsheet, the function that adds a column only in the rows meeting conditions is ___.
hint: Its name is the plural of a sum with conditions.

prompt: You open faro.csv and every row sits in column A. What happened?
hint: Look at the import dialog.

choices.text: The file is corrupted and has to be copied again
choices.why: The text is intact; the spreadsheet split it in the wrong place.

choices.text: The encoding is not UTF-8, so the columns merged
choices.why: That garbles accents; it does not merge columns.

choices.text: The separator was guessed wrong
choices.why: Choose comma, and nothing else, in the import dialog.

choices.text: The formulas are formatted as text
choices.why: That shows a formula as text, after the import.

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend LibreOffice over the online option for this course?
hint: Think about whose data you will use.

choices.text: Your files stay on your own computer
choices.why: That matters when the analysis is your employer's data; the formulas were also checked in it.

choices.text: It has more chart types
choices.why: The lesson does not compare chart types.

choices.text: Online tools cannot open CSV files, only their own formats
choices.why: They can. The difference is where the files live.

choices.text: Employers require it
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

prompt: Marina is preparing next month's meeting. Which changes follow from this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Attention, meaning, a request.

choices.text: Titles that state the finding
choices.why: That buys attention.

choices.text: A slide saying what the 41.5% costs the people in the room
choices.why: That is So what? in the audience's terms.

choices.text: A closing slide that asks for a decision
choices.why: That is the request the first meeting never had.

choices.text: Every cohort table, so nobody can say data is missing
choices.why: Data was never what the room lacked; the tables go to an appendix.
